title: Bēowulf
titleEn: Beowulf — Fitt XVIII: The Queen’s Necklace (lines 1192–1250)
source: Fr. Klaeber, Beowulf and the Fight at Finnsburg, 1st edition (Boston: D. C. Heath & Co., 1922), pp. 45–47, lines 1192–1250 (fitt XVIII). Text follows Klaeber's printing exactly — þ, ð, æ, vowel-length macrons, a circumflex for contracted vowels (Klaeber prints one mark over the pair of vowels; we place it on the second), [brackets] for letters or words added by emendation, (parentheses) for conjectural restoration of fire-damaged letters, and Klaeber's rows of dots where words are lost. A dot under a vowel (dōgọra) is Klaeber's sign that the vowel does not count in the metre. Transcribed from the page images of the archive.org scan, every page read twice. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed late West Saxon, c. 1000, following Campbell's Old English Grammar — and the recorded reading follows it, within stated limits. No synthetic voice for Old English exists, so the reading is produced by an American English neural voice under per-word phonetic pinning: every sound is specified outright rather than left to modern English habits. So æ is the vowel of 'cat' and a the open back vowel of 'father'; short and long vowels stay apart; ea and eo are sounded as two-part diphthongs; sc is 'sh', cg the 'j' of 'edge', hw a breathy w; h after a vowel is the rasp of German 'ach' or 'ich'; and doubled consonants are held long. The limits: the voice has no throaty g (dagas, lagu), so it says a plain g; long ǣ, long ȳ and long ēa are heard short; compounds are not split, so a sound at the seam of a compound is occasionally voiced where it should not be; and unstressed vowels keep their full quality. The reading is a model of one scholarly convention, as much a reconstruction as the text. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, which was scorched in a library fire in 1731; its edges have crumbled away, and some readings survive only in two transcripts made in 1787. What you read here is a reconstruction — Klaeber's edition of 1922 — and parts of it are educated guesswork: [brackets] mark letters editors added, (parentheses) mark letters restored where the manuscript is damaged or lost, and a few words are best guesses whose exact meaning no one knows. The notes say so where it matters. Line numbers are Klaeber's, the standard way of citing the poem.

sentences.t:
Him wæs ful boren, ond frēondlaþu
wordum bewægned, ond wunden gold
ēstum geēawed, earm[h]rēade twā,
sentences.l: To him was a cup borne, and friendly invitation with words offered, and wound gold with favors shown, two arm-ornaments,
sentences.i: A cup was carried to him, and a friendly welcome offered in words, and twisted gold graciously displayed: two arm-rings,
sentences.n: ‘Him’ is dative, ‘to him’ (Beowulf, whom the queen has come to), and ‘wæs … boren’ is a passive, ‘was borne’; the things brought are ‘ful’ (a cup), ‘frēondlaþu’ (a friendly invitation) and ‘wunden gold’ (twisted, wound gold). ‘bewægned’ is the participle of a verb found nowhere else in the poem, and ‘offered’ is a guess from the context. ‘ēstum’ is dative plural of ‘ēst’ (favor, grace), ‘with graces’, and ‘geēawed’ is ‘shown, displayed’. The word ‘earm[h]rēade’ is an emendation: the manuscript has ‘reade’, and Grein supplies the ‘h’ to make ‘earmhrēade’, ‘arm-ornaments’ (‘twā’, ‘two’, goes with it); ‘hrēad’ is itself rare, and ‘twisted’ is not in the word, so ‘arm-rings’ is a guess.

sentences.t:
hrægl ond hringas, healsbēaga mǣst
þāra þe ic on foldan gefrægen hæbbe.
sentences.l: garment and rings, of neck-rings the greatest of those that I on earth have heard tell of.
sentences.i: a robe and rings, the greatest neck-ornament of all that I have ever heard of on earth.
sentences.n: ‘hrægl ond hringas’ continue the list of gifts. ‘healsbēaga’ is the genitive plural of ‘healsbēag’ (‘neck-ring’), dependent on ‘mǣst’ (superlative of ‘micel’, ‘greatest’), so ‘greatest of neck-rings’; ‘þāra þe’ is ‘of those which’. ‘gefrægen hæbbe’ is the perfect of ‘gefrignan’, ‘learn by asking, hear of’ (‘hæbbe’ looks the same in the indicative and the subjunctive; the subjunctive is usual in a relative clause after a superlative): ‘ic’ is the poet, who often says he knows things only by report.

sentences.t:
Nǣnigne ic under swegle sēlran hȳrde
hordmāðụm hæleþa,
sentences.l: No better under the sky have I heard of, among hoard-treasures of heroes,
sentences.i: I have heard of no better among the hoarded treasures of heroes under heaven,
sentences.n: ‘Nǣnigne’ is accusative singular masculine, ‘no’, and goes with ‘sēlran’ (‘better’, the weak comparative of ‘gōd’); the noun they agree with is left unspoken, ‘no better one’, and the phrase is the object of ‘hȳrde’ (‘heard of’). The idiomatic version leaves the noun unspoken too. ‘hordmāðụm’ has a dot under the ‘u’; this is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, and it changes nothing in the sense. The word is dative plural, ‘among hoard-treasures’ (‘hord’ hoard, ‘māðum’ treasure), and ‘hæleþa’ is ‘of heroes’. ‘under swegle’ is ‘under the sky’. The manuscript has two words here, ‘mad mum’, which editors join and mend.

sentences.t:
syþðan Hāma ætwæg
tō þǣre byrhtan byrig Brōsinga mene,
sigle ond sincfæt, —
sentences.l: since Hama carried off to the bright stronghold the Brosings’ necklace, jewel and treasure-vessel, —
sentences.i: ever since Hama bore off to the shining stronghold the Brosings’ necklace, the jewel and treasure-vessel, —
sentences.n: ‘syþðan’ is ‘since’; Hama is the subject of ‘ætwæg’ (past of ‘ætwegan’, ‘carry off’). He is a hero of Germanic legend, and the Brosings (‘Brōsinga’, genitive plural) are a legendary people whose necklace (‘mene’, accusative) was famous; Grimm and Bugge would print ‘Brīsinga’ (apparatus). ‘tō þǣre byrhtan byrig’ is ‘to the bright stronghold’; ‘þǣre’ is Klaeber’s, the manuscript having ‘here’. ‘sigle’ (jewel, brooch) and ‘sincfæt’ (‘sinc’ treasure + ‘fæt’ vessel) are in apposition to ‘mene’. Why a necklace is also a ‘vessel’ is unclear; ‘a setting for jewels’ is a guess. The dash opens a digression about Hama.

sentences.t:
searonīðas flēah
Eormenrīces, gecēas ēcne rǣd. —
sentences.l: he fled the cunning-hatreds of Eormenric, chose lasting counsel. —
sentences.i: he escaped the treacherous malice of Eormenric and chose the course that lasts. —
sentences.n: A crux. The manuscript has ‘fealh’, which makes no sense here; Leo and Grundtvig read ‘flēah’ (past of ‘flēon’, ‘flee’), which takes the accusative ‘searonīðas’ (‘searu’ trick, cunning + ‘nīð’ hatred, so ‘cunning-hatreds’, malice). Eormenric (genitive) is the legendary tyrant king of the Goths. ‘gecēas’ is the past of ‘gecēosan’, ‘choose’, and ‘ēcne rǣd’ is ‘eternal, lasting counsel’; ‘rǣd’ can mean counsel, plan or advantage. What Hama chose is not said, and ‘a lasting course’ is a guess; some read it as a turn to God. The dash ends the digression.

sentences.t:
Þone hring hæfde Higelāc Gēata,
nefa Swertinges nȳhstan sīðe,
sentences.l: That ring had Higelac of the Geats, nephew of Swerting, on his latest journey,
sentences.i: Higelac of the Geats, Swerting’s nephew, had that ring on his last expedition,
sentences.n: ‘Þone hring’ is the accusative object put first, ‘that ring’, the necklace of the digression; ‘hæfde’ is ‘had’, Higelāc the subject, Beowulf’s lord. ‘nefa Swertinges’ is ‘nephew of Swerting’; ‘nefa’ can also mean ‘grandson’, and Swerting is named nowhere else in the poem, so who he was is unknown. ‘nȳhstan sīðe’ is a dative of time, ‘on his nearest, last journey’ (‘nȳhsta’ is the superlative of ‘nēah’).

sentences.t:
siðþan hē under segne sinc ealgode,
wælrēaf werede;
sentences.l: after he under the banner treasure defended, slain-spoil guarded;
sentences.i: when, beneath his banner, he defended his treasure and guarded the spoil taken from the slain;
sentences.n: ‘under segne’ is ‘under the banner’ (dative). ‘ealgode’ and ‘werede’ are past singular, ‘defended’ and ‘guarded’, with ‘sinc’ and ‘wælrēaf’ (‘wæl’ the slain + ‘rēaf’ plunder, so ‘slain-spoil’) as objects. ‘werede’ could come from ‘werian’ ‘wear’ as easily as ‘werian’ ‘defend’; I take ‘guard’ because it runs parallel to ‘ealgode’, but ‘wore the spoil of the slain’ is possible.

sentences.t:
hyne wyrd fornam,
syþðan hē for wlenco wēan āhsode,
fǣhðe tō Frȳsum.
sentences.l: him fate took off, after he out of pride woe asked for, feud against the Frisians.
sentences.i: fate took him off, after he had, in his pride, sought out misery: a feud with the Frisians.
sentences.n: ‘hyne’ is the accusative ‘him’, ‘wyrd’ (fate) the subject, ‘fornam’ the past of ‘forniman’, ‘take away, destroy’. ‘for wlenco’ is ‘out of pride’ (dative of ‘wlenco’: pride, high spirits, wealth). ‘āhsode’ is the past of ‘āhsian’, ‘ask for, seek out’ (the same word as ‘ask’), so ‘wēan āhsode’ is ‘asked for woe’, and ‘fǣhðe’ (a feud) stands in apposition. ‘tō Frȳsum’ is ‘against the Frisians’. This is Higelac’s fatal raid on the Frisians, which the poem returns to later.

sentences.l: He those ornaments bore, eorclan-stones, over the wave-cup, the mighty prince;
sentences.i: The mighty prince bore those treasures, the precious stones, over the sea;
sentences.n: ‘wæg’ is the past of ‘wegan’, ‘carry’; ‘frætwe’ is accusative plural, ‘ornaments, treasures’. ‘eorclanstānas’ is printed as in the manuscript; Grundtvig reads ‘eorcnanstānas’ (apparatus), and ‘eorcnanstān’ is the usual word for a precious stone, so ‘eorclan-’ is probably a slip for it. ‘ȳða ful’ is ‘the cup of the waves’ (‘ȳða’ genitive plural), a kenning for the sea; it is the same word ‘ful’ as the cup at the opening of the fitt. ‘rīce þēoden’ is ‘mighty prince’, in apposition to ‘Hē’.

sentences.t: hē under rande gecranc.
sentences.l: he under shield fell.
sentences.i: he fell beneath his shield.
sentences.n: ‘rande’ is the dative of ‘rand’ (shield-rim, shield), and ‘under rande’ is ‘under the shield’, that is, in battle; ‘gecranc’ is the past of ‘gecringan’, ‘fall in battle’. The prince of the last unit is Higelac himself.

sentences.t:
Gehwearf þā in Francna fæþm feorh cyninges,
brēostgewǣdu, ond se bēah somod;
sentences.l: Turned then into the Franks’ embrace the king’s life, breast-garments, and the ring together;
sentences.i: Then the king’s life passed into the Franks’ grasp, with his breast-armor and the ring together;
sentences.n: ‘Gehwearf’ is the past singular of ‘gehweorfan’, ‘turn, pass’, and its subject is ‘feorh cyninges’ (‘king’s life’, nominative), with ‘brēostgewǣdu’ (‘breast-garments’, that is, his mail) and ‘se bēah’ added. ‘in Francna fæþm’ is ‘into the Franks’ embrace’ (accusative, after a verb of motion). Sievers proposed ‘feoh’ (wealth) for ‘feorh’ (apparatus); Klaeber keeps ‘feorh’, so the king’s life and his gear pass together. ‘somod’ is ‘together’.

sentences.t:
wyrsan wīgfrecan wæl rēafedon
æfter gūðsceare,
sentences.l: worse warriors the slain plundered after the battle-shearing,
sentences.i: men of less worth stripped the slain after the slaughter,
sentences.n: ‘wyrsan’ is the comparative ‘worse’, nominative plural, with ‘wīgfrecan’ (‘war-bold ones’, warriors), so lesser men; ‘wæl’ is accusative, ‘the slain’. ‘rēafedon’ is Klaeber’s correction: the manuscript has ‘reafeden’, a subjunctive ending, and he makes it the plain past plural. ‘gūðsceare’ is dative of ‘gūðscearu’ (feminine), ‘battle-shearing’, the hewing of battle; Holtzmann reads ‘gūðceare’, ‘battle-sorrow’.

sentences.t:
Gēata lēode
hrēawīc hēoldon. —
sentences.l: the Geats’ people the corpse-place held. —
sentences.i: and the people of the Geats held the field of corpses. —
sentences.n: With Klaeber’s punctuation, ‘Gēata lēode’ (nominative plural) is the subject of ‘hēoldon’, and ‘hrēawīc’ (‘hrēaw’ corpse + ‘wīc’ dwelling, place) is the object: ‘held the corpse-place’. Since the Geats lost, ‘held’ may mean that they lay dead on it; that is a guess. Several editors put the comma after ‘lēode’, so that ‘Gēata lēode’ belongs with the plundering (‘plundered the Geats’ dead’) and someone else holds the field. The dash closes the aside.

sentences.t: Heal swēge onfēng.
sentences.l: The hall sound received.
sentences.i: The hall took up the sound.
sentences.n: ‘Heal’ (hall, nominative) is the subject, and ‘swēge’ is the dative object of ‘onfēng’ (past of ‘onfōn’, ‘receive, take up’). ‘swēg’ is sound, noise or music, so the line says that the hall took up the noise of the company once the digression was over, a guess at the poet’s picture. Cosijn would read ‘healsbēge’ (that is, ‘healsbēage’, ‘neck-ring’) in place of ‘Heal swēge’ (apparatus); Klaeber keeps the hall and the sound.

sentences.t: Wealhðēo maþelode, hēo fore þǣm werede spræc:
sentences.l: Wealhtheow spoke in speech-words, she before the troop spoke:
sentences.i: Wealhtheow spoke in formal words; she spoke before the company:
sentences.n: ‘maþelode’ is the house formula for a formal speech (‘spoke in speech-words’), and the colon announces what she says. ‘Wealhðēo’ is the queen, Hrothgar’s wife; ‘hēo’ is ‘she’, ‘fore þǣm werede’ is ‘before the troop’ (dative), and ‘spræc’ the past of ‘sprecan’. She now addresses Beowulf directly.

sentences.t:
‘Brūc ðisses bēages, Bēowulf lēofa,
hyse, mid hǣle, ond þisses hrægles nēot,
sentences.l: ‘Enjoy this ring, dear Beowulf, young man, with good luck, and of this garment make use,
sentences.i: ‘Enjoy this ring with good fortune, dear Beowulf, young man, and make use of this robe,
sentences.n: ‘Brūc’ and ‘nēot’ are imperatives of ‘brūcan’ and ‘nēotan’, both taking the genitive, so ‘ðisses bēages’ and ‘þisses hrægles’ are ‘of this ring’, ‘of this garment’. ‘Bēowulf lēofa’ and ‘hyse’ (‘youth’) are vocatives. ‘mid hǣle’ is ‘with health, with good luck’.

sentences.t: þēo[d]gestrēona,
sentences.l: of the people’s treasures,
sentences.i: and of the nation’s treasures,
sentences.n: The genitive plural ‘þēodgestrēona’ (‘þēod’ people + ‘gestrēon’ treasure) comes straight after ‘nēot’, which takes the genitive, so the plainest reading is a second object of ‘nēot’: make use of the robe and of the nation’s treasures. It could instead be a loose phrase saying that ring and robe are among the nation’s great treasures; that is a guess, and I take the first. The ‘d’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has ‘þeo’, and the word is completed after Grundtvig’s translation and Kemble.

sentences.t:
ond geþēoh tela,
cen þec mid cræfte,
sentences.l: and thrive well, make known yourself with skill,
sentences.i: and prosper well; show yourself by your skill,
sentences.n: ‘geþēoh’ is the imperative of ‘geþēon’, ‘thrive’, with ‘tela’ (‘well’). ‘cen’ is the imperative of ‘cennan’, ‘make known, show’, and ‘þec’ is the accusative ‘you’ (the older form beside ‘þē’), the object of ‘cen’ and reflexive in sense, so the sense is ‘show yourself, show what you are’; ‘cræfte’ is a dative of means, ‘skill’ or ‘strength’, and I leave the word as ‘skill’. The line is the queen’s blessing before her request.

sentences.t:
ond þyssum cnyhtum wes
lāra līðe!
sentences.l: and to these boys be of counsels gentle!
sentences.i: and be gentle in your counsel to these boys!
sentences.n: ‘cnyhtum’ is the dative plural of ‘cniht’, ‘boys’, presumably her sons sitting near. ‘wes’ is imperative of ‘wesan’; ‘lāra’ is a genitive of respect (‘lār’ counsel, teaching) and ‘līðe’ is ‘gentle, kind’, so ‘gentle in counsel’. She asks him to be a kindly adviser to the young princes.

sentences.t: Ic þē þæs lēan geman.
sentences.l: I for you for that reward remember.
sentences.i: I will not forget to reward you for that.
sentences.n: ‘geman’ is the present of ‘gemunan’, ‘remember’, with a future sense, and ‘þē’ is dative, ‘to you’. ‘þæs’ is genitive, ‘for that’, and ‘lēan’ (accusative) is ‘reward’, so ‘I keep a reward in mind for you for that’. What ‘that’ is is not said; the context points to his clearing Heorot of Grendel.

sentences.t:
Hafast þū gefēred, þæt ðē feor ond nēah
ealne wīdeferhþ weras ehtigað,
efne swā sīde swā sǣ bebūgeð
windgeard weallas.
sentences.l: You have brought it about that men esteem you far and near, all your wide-life, just as widely as the sea encircles the wind-yard, the walls.
sentences.i: You have brought it about that men will honor you far and near, for all time, as widely as the sea encircles the windy world, its shores.
sentences.n: ‘Hafast … gefēred’ is the perfect of ‘gefēran’, ‘bring about’, and the ‘þæt’-clause says what he has brought about: men (‘weras’) ‘ehtigað’ him. I take ‘ehtigað’ from ‘eahtian’, ‘esteem, praise’, not ‘ehtan’, ‘pursue’, since the sense needs honor. ‘ealne wīdeferhþ’ is an accusative of time, ‘all the wide life’, that is, always. ‘ehtigað’ is present tense; ‘will honor’ in the idiomatic version gives it the forward look of the sentence. ‘efne swā sīde swā’ is ‘just as widely as’. The last words are disputed. The manuscript has ‘wind geard weallas’; Klaeber (after Krackow) keeps ‘windgeard’ (‘wind-yard’, the windy world) with ‘weallas’ (‘walls’, shores) in apposition. Other editors divide the letters as ‘windge eardweallas’ or ‘windige weallas’ (‘windy shores’); the apparatus lists them, and my version is only one reading.

sentences.t:
Wes þenden þū lifige,
æþeling, ēadig!
sentences.l: Be, while you live, prince, blessed!
sentences.i: May you be fortunate, prince, as long as you live!
sentences.n: ‘Wes’ is the imperative of ‘wesan’, ‘þenden þū lifige’ is ‘while you live’ with the subjunctive, and ‘ēadig’ is ‘blessed, prosperous’. ‘æþeling’ is a vocative, ‘prince, noble one’. The apparatus notes that several editors omit the comma after it.

sentences.t:
Ic þē an tela
sincgestrēona.
sentences.l: I grant you well of treasure-possessions.
sentences.i: I gladly grant you treasures.
sentences.n: ‘an’ is the present singular of ‘unnan’, ‘grant, not begrudge’, which takes a dative of the person (‘þē’) and a genitive of the thing (‘sincgestrēona’, ‘treasure-possessions’, genitive plural); ‘tela’ is ‘well’. She speaks of the gifts she has just given.

sentences.t:
Bēo þū suna mīnum
dǣdum gedēfe, drēamhealdende!
sentences.l: Be you to my son in deeds kind, joy-holding!
sentences.i: Be kind to my son in all you do, and hold fast to gladness!
sentences.n: ‘Bēo’ is the imperative of ‘wesan’. ‘suna’ is the dative singular of ‘sunu’, ‘to my son’, although ‘cnyhtum’ was plural a few lines back; the singular is printed as it stands. ‘dǣdum’ is dative plural, ‘in deeds’, and ‘gedēfe’ is ‘fitting, gentle’. ‘drēamhealdende’ (‘drēam’ joy + a present participle of ‘healdan’, ‘hold’) occurs only here; ‘joy-holding’ is literal, and ‘holding fast to gladness’ is a guess at what it asks of him.

sentences.t: Hēr is ǣghwylc eorl ōþrum getrȳwe,
sentences.l: Here is each man to the other true,
sentences.i: Here every man is true to the other,
sentences.n: ‘Hēr is’ points to the hall. ‘ǣghwylc eorl’ is ‘each man’ (nominative), ‘ōþrum’ is dative, ‘to the other’, and ‘getrȳwe’ is ‘true, loyal’. She is assuring Beowulf of the loyalty of the company in the hall.

sentences.t: mōdes milde, mandrihtne hol[d],
sentences.l: mild of mind, to his lord loyal,
sentences.i: gentle in heart, loyal to their lord,
sentences.n: ‘mōdes’ is a genitive of respect, ‘in mind’, with ‘milde’ (‘mild’); ‘mandrihtne’ is dative, ‘to the liege-lord’. The ‘d’ of ‘hol[d]’ is Klaeber’s: the manuscript has ‘hol’, altered from ‘heol’, and Thorkelin and Kemble complete it as ‘hold’, ‘loyal’.

sentences.t:
þegnas syndon geþwǣre, þēod ealgearo,
druncne dryhtguman;
sentences.l: thanes are in accord, the people all-ready, drunken troop-men;
sentences.i: the thanes are of one mind, the people ready, the company drunk;
sentences.n: ‘þegnas’ is the nominative plural, ‘thanes’, and ‘geþwǣre’ is ‘in harmony, of one mind’. ‘ealgearo’ is ‘wholly ready’. ‘druncne dryhtguman’ is ‘drunken troop-men’ (‘dryht’ retinue + ‘guma’ man), in apposition to the others; she says they are drunk but willing.

sentences.t: dō swā ic bidde!’
sentences.l: do as I ask!’
sentences.i: do as I ask!”
sentences.n: ‘dō’ is Klaeber’s correction (after Sievers): the manuscript has ‘doð’, which could be a plural imperative or an indicative, and the singular ‘dō’ makes it a plain imperative to Beowulf alone. ‘bidde’ is the first singular present of ‘biddan’, ‘ask’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: Ēode þā tō setle.
sentences.l: Went then to the seat.
sentences.i: Then she went to her seat.
sentences.n: ‘Ēode’ is the past of ‘gān’, ‘go’; the subject, the queen, is not repeated. ‘tō setle’ is ‘to her seat’ (dative of ‘setl’).

sentences.t:
Þǣr wæs symbla cyst,
druncon wīn weras.
sentences.l: There was the best of feasts, drank wine the men.
sentences.i: There was the finest of feasts, and the men drank wine.
sentences.n: ‘symbla cyst’ is ‘the best of feasts’ (‘symbla’ genitive plural, ‘cyst’ nominative: choice, pick); ‘druncon’ is the past plural of ‘drincan’, with ‘wīn’ as object and ‘weras’ as subject. The two clauses are set side by side without a conjunction.

sentences.t:
Wyrd ne cūþon,
geōsceaft grimme, swā hit āgangen wearð
eorla manegum,
sentences.l: Fate they did not know, the grim ordained-lot, as it had come to pass for many of the men,
sentences.i: They did not know their fate, the grim decree, as it had come about for many of the men,
sentences.n: ‘Wyrd’ and ‘geōsceaft’ are accusatives, objects of ‘ne cūþon’ (‘did not know’, past plural of ‘cunnan’). ‘geōsceaft’ is a feminine noun, ‘what was ordained’, so ‘ordained-lot’; its first part is obscure, and Kluge and Holthausen would print ‘geasceaft’ (apparatus). ‘grimme’ is Klaeber’s change from the manuscript’s ‘grimne’, because a feminine accusative needs ‘-e’. ‘swā hit āgangen wearð’ is ‘as it had come to pass’; ‘eorla manegum’ is a dative, ‘for many of the men’. The poet looks ahead to the night’s killing.

sentences.t:
syþðan ǣfen cwōm,
ond him Hrōþgār gewāt tō hofe sīnum,
rīce tō ræste.
sentences.l: after evening came, and Hrothgar went off to his house, the mighty one to rest.
sentences.i: when evening came, and Hrothgar went off to his house, the mighty king to his rest.
sentences.n: ‘cwōm’ is a variant of ‘cōm’, ‘came’; ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, ‘gewāt … him’ ‘went off’; ‘hofe sīnum’ is ‘to his dwelling’ (dative), and ‘rīce’ (‘mighty’, nominative) is a noun-use, ‘the mighty one’. The apparatus notes that several editors begin a new sentence at ‘syþðan’ and end it at ‘ræste’, and that one editor carries it on to line 1238; Klaeber joins it to the sentence about fate.

sentences.t:
Reced weardode
unrīm eorla, swā hīe oft ǣr dydon.
sentences.l: A countless number of men guarded the hall, as they often before did.
sentences.i: Countless warriors kept watch over the hall, as they had often done before.
sentences.n: ‘unrīm’ is a neuter noun, ‘a countless number’, with the genitive ‘eorla’, and the verb ‘weardode’ is singular to match it. ‘swā hīe oft ǣr dydon’ has ‘dydon’ as the past plural of ‘dōn’: ‘as they often did before’.

sentences.t: Bencþelu beredon;
sentences.l: They cleared the bench-planks;
sentences.i: They cleared the boards beside the benches;
sentences.n: ‘Bencþelu’ (‘bench-planks’, the floor by the benches) is the object of ‘beredon’. I take ‘beredon’ as the past plural of ‘berian’, ‘make bare, clear’, a guess from the sentence that follows, where the floor is covered over.

sentences.t:
hit geondbrǣded wearð
beddum ond bolstrum.
sentences.l: it was spread over with beds and bolsters.
sentences.i: it was spread over with beds and bolsters.
sentences.n: ‘hit’ is the floor, and ‘geondbrǣded’ is the participle of ‘geondbrǣdan’, ‘spread over’; ‘beddum ond bolstrum’ are datives plural of means, ‘with beds and bolsters’.

sentences.t:
Bēorscealca sum
fūs ond fǣge fletræste gebēag.
sentences.l: Of the beer-men one, ready and doomed, to hall-rest bowed.
sentences.i: One of the beer-drinkers, ready for bed and fated to die, lay down to rest in the hall.
sentences.n: ‘sum’ with the genitive plural ‘bēorscealca’ is ‘one of the …’. ‘bēorscealc’ is ‘bēor’ beer + ‘scealc’ (servant, man), a man at the beer; whether a cup-bearer or a carouser, I cannot tell. ‘fūs’ is ‘ready, eager’, ‘fǣge’ is ‘fated to die’ (‘fey’), and ‘fletræste gebēag’ is ‘bowed to the hall-bed’ (‘flet’ hall floor + ‘ræst’ rest; ‘gebēag’ past of ‘gebūgan’). He is not named; ‘fǣge’ marks him as one whose death is near, though the poem does not say here that he dies.

sentences.t:
Setton him tō hēafdon hilderandas,
bordwudu beorhtan;
sentences.l: They set to themselves at their heads battle-shields, bright board-wood;
sentences.i: They set their battle-shields at their heads, the bright shield-wood;
sentences.n: ‘Setton’ is the past plural of ‘settan’; ‘him’ is a reflexive dative, ‘for themselves’; ‘tō hēafdon’ is ‘at their heads’. ‘hilderandas’ (‘hild’ battle + ‘rand’ shield) is accusative plural, and ‘bordwudu beorhtan’ (‘board-wood’, a shield) repeats it.

sentences.t:
þǣr on bence wæs
ofer æþelinge ȳþgesēne
heaþostēapa helm, hringed byrne,
þrecwudu þrymlīc.
sentences.l: There on the bench was, above the prince, easy to see, the battle-lofty helmet, ringed mail-coat, strength-wood glorious.
sentences.i: There on the bench above the nobleman could be seen the lofty helmet, the ringed mail-coat and the splendid spear.
sentences.n: ‘helm’, ‘byrne’ and ‘þrecwudu’ are the subjects of ‘wæs’. ‘heaþostēapa’ is ‘battle-lofty’ (‘heaðo’ battle + ‘stēap’ high; the exact sense is uncertain), a weak adjective in the nominative singular masculine agreeing with ‘helm’. ‘hringed’ is ‘ringed’. ‘þrecwudu’ is ‘strength-wood’ (‘þræc’ force + ‘wudu’ wood), which I take to be a spear; that is a guess from the first part. ‘ȳþgesēne’ cannot agree with the dative ‘æþelinge’ (the ending would be ‘-um’), so it says that the gear was ‘easy to see’. ‘ofer æþelinge’ is ‘above the prince’; the noun is singular, and I take it to mean each sleeper’s gear above his own place, which is a guess.

sentences.t:
Wæs þēaw hyra,
þæt hīe oft wǣron an wīg gearwe,
gē æt hām gē on herge, gē gehwæþer þāra
efne swylce mǣla, swylce hira mandryhtne
þearf gesǣlde;
sentences.l: It was their custom, that they often were ready for war, both at home and in the host, both each of them just at such times as to their liege-lord need befell;
sentences.i: It was their custom to be ready for war often, both at home and on campaign, and each of them at just such times as their lord had need;
sentences.n: ‘Wæs þēaw hyra’ is ‘their custom was’, and ‘hyra’ is the genitive plural ‘their’. ‘an wīg gearwe’ is ‘ready for war’ (‘an’ is a spelling of ‘on’); some editors print one word ‘ānwīggearwe’, ‘ready for single combat’. ‘gē … gē’ is ‘both … and’; the apparatus notes that some editors delete the second ‘gē’. ‘gehwæþer þāra’ is ‘each of them’, ‘efne swylce mǣla’ ‘at just such times’ (genitive plural of ‘mǣl’), and ‘gesǣlde’ is past singular, ‘befell’ (the indicative and the subjunctive look alike here): the men were ready whenever their lord had need.

sentences.t: wæs sēo þēod tilu.
sentences.l: was that people good.
sentences.i: That was a worthy people.
sentences.n: ‘tilu’ is the nominative singular feminine of ‘til’, ‘good, serviceable, worthy’, agreeing with ‘þēod’ (people). The fitt ends on this note of approval, just before the attack.
